title: Holding your hem
hook: leaving praise and blame, I have caught hold of Your hem, sung as the couple takes the scarf (Ramkali ki Var M5, ang 963)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lav 4, and your line: round four: union. Did you sit with someone and let it be easy? Today we step back to the start of the wedding, to the moment just before the first round. Day six hundred sixty-six.

Before the four rounds begin, there's a small gesture that's easy to miss. The groom has a long scarf over his shoulder. The bride's father stands, takes one end of it, and places it in his daughter's hand. That's all. Nobody makes a speech. But the musicians are singing a line as it happens, and if you know the words, the gesture changes. Because the line isn't about the groom at all.
screen: `A SCARF OVER THE GROOM'S SHOULDER.` → `THE FATHER PLACES ONE END.` → `THE LINE BEING SUNG.`

segments.voice: The scarf is called the palla. The shabad sung while it's placed comes from Guru Arjan's Var in Raag Ramkali, on Ang nine sixty-three. In paraphrase, it says: praise and slander, I have given them all up; I have let everything go. I have seen that all relationships are false, so I have caught hold of Your hem. Read that slowly, and it's startling to sing at a wedding. All relationships are false? On the day two families join? But the singer isn't the bride speaking to the groom. In Gurbani the soul is often the bride and God the Husband. The one whose hem she grabs is the Lord. So the shabad reminds everyone in the room of something tender and a little fierce: the deepest thing to hold on to, the shabad says, isn't another person, even this beloved person. It's the One. One reading draws a lesson for the marriage too: two people who each hold God's hem aren't asking each other to be everything. Then look at what's let go first: praise and slander. Ustat and nindaa. What people say about you, good or bad. A wedding is full of it: the clothes, the food, the gossip about the in-laws. The shabad drops all of it before the first step. The palla itself is just cloth. But held in a bride's hand, with that line in the air, it becomes a picture of a soul taking hold of what won't let go. The couple will walk the four rounds holding it, so neither walks alone.
screen: `THE PALLA: THE WEDDING SCARF.` · `PRAISE AND SLANDER, LET GO.` · `THE HEM IS THE LORD'S.` · `TWO WHO EACH HOLD ON TO GOD.` · then, large: `HOLDING THE HEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a loved one's hand. If someone you love is near, take their hand for a moment, without needing to say why. If no one is near, hold your own hands together, or hold something that belongs to someone you love: a scarf, a ring, a photo. Feel the simple fact of holding on. Then, gently, let go of one thing people say about you, good or bad, that you've been carrying. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you hold. The bell holds the time.
Holding your hem. Guru Arjan's line, sung as the bride takes the palla: letting go of praise and slander, the soul catches hold of the Lord's hem.
Your line: holding the hem. Today, when praise or criticism comes your way, let it pass, and notice what you're really holding on to. Day six hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: At an Anand Karaj, while the bride's father places one end of the groom's palla in her hand, ragis sing Guru Arjan's line about letting go of praise and slander and holding the Lord's hem.

match.prompt: the scarf and the hem — tap the pairs.
pairs: places the scarf in her hand

myth: the line sung at the palla is the bride speaking to the groom
the soul is the bride, and the hem she holds is the Lord's.
the shabad lets go of both praise and slander
ustat and nindaa: what people say, good or bad, is given up first.

fork.setup: the musicians sing, 'I have caught hold of Your hem.' whose hem does the shabad mean?
fork.reveal: in Gurbani the soul is the bride and God the Husband: the hem is the Lord's, even as the bride holds the groom's scarf.

original.note: Punjabi: the end of a scarf, a hem; the palla joins the couple through the four rounds.

trapdoor: what you thought: the scarf is a symbol of the bride belonging to the groom.
what it means: the line sung with it is about the soul holding God's hem, letting go of praise and blame.
what a scholar hears: the salok comes from Guru Arjan's Ramkali ki Var (Ang 963), where 'all relationships are false' sets up the turn to the Lord.

sources.ref: Ramkali ki Var Mahalla 5, salok (ustat nindaa naanak jee mai habh vanjaaee), Ang 963

notes: Salok paraphrased: praise and slander given up, everything abandoned, all relations seen as false, so I hold Your hem. Confirm the paraphrase and that it is the salok sung at the palla ceremony.
Custom that the bride's father places the palla in her hand: widely practiced, but details vary; confirm wording.
Gurmukhi spelling given in modern Punjabi (ਪੱਲਾ); the shabad's own form is ਪਲੈ. Confirm which is better for the original game.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the stock 'makes grandmothers cry' and the unsourced scarf colors; 'Sikh teachers say that's exactly what makes a marriage safe' recast as one reading; the line about what 'you' hold on to is now the shabad's claim; dropped the repeated 'Today: …' hook ending.
